activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: French speakers ask a price with "C'est combien ?" or "Combien ça coûte ?", both meaning "How much is it?"
story:
Easton dug through his backpack on his grandfather's tiled porch, trying to excavate his pocket money from under a paperback and a tangle of earbuds. He came up with eight euros in coins, which should have been plenty, but he could not be sure, because he had never once ordered anything in French. Across the courtyard, his grandfather's kitchen window stood open, and the smell of coffee drifted out into the warm afternoon.

"Are you going to stare at your money all day?" Tristan called from the gate. Tristan had spent two summers at this house before and had one clear goal: to reach the crêpe stand in the square before the best flavors sold out, and he wanted Easton to do the ordering for both of them. "You promised. You've been practicing all week."

"I've been practicing words," Easton said, pocketing the coins. "Saying them to an actual person is different." His assumption had been that everyone at the stand would switch to English the moment he stumbled, which would make the whole thing pointless. Tristan shrugged and said that had not happened to him last year, so they would find out.

The square was quiet, with plane trees dropping dappled light onto the stone, and the crêpe stand had a short line. Easton listened while he waited. The man ahead of them, a local, pointed at a crêpe and asked, "C'est combien ?" and the vendor answered with a price. Then a woman at the other end of the counter asked, "Combien ça coûte ?" about a bottle of cider, and got an answer too. Two different questions, Easton thought, and the vendor had treated them the same way, so both must mean "How much is it?" He filed that away like a coin he could actually spend.

When their turn came, Easton stepped up. "Bonjour. Un crêpe au chocolat, s'il vous plaît," he said, and the words came out steadier than he expected. The vendor nodded and started pouring batter. Easton hesitated, then tried it. "C'est combien ?"

"Quatre euros cinquante," the vendor said. Easton did the math quickly. Four fifty for his, and Tristan wanted lemon and sugar, probably cheaper, so his eight euros would cover both with change to spare. He ordered the second crêpe, paid, and collected the warm paper sleeves.

"You did it," Tristan said, already tearing off a corner of his crêpe. "Better than my first try, honestly."

"Next time I'm going to try it the other way," Easton said, taking a bite. "Combien ça coûte?" He pointed at a bottle of cider sitting by the counter, and the vendor laughed and told him.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
The mirror in the girls' bathroom had told the truth that morning, and the truth had three red bumps along Rebecca's chin. Nothing like this had happened last year, which was the part that bugged her most. She spent all of math class sketching a timeline in her notebook: smooth skin in September, one tiny bump in February, three bumps now. Something had changed, and she meant to find out what.

After school she marched into Murphy's Pharmacy with her allowance crumpled in her pocket. Maddox had promised to meet her there, and he was already leaning against the shelf of face washes like he'd been waiting for hours.

"They multiply at night," Rebecca whispered, pointing at her chin. "Every morning there's more. It's like they're nocturnal."

Maddox peered at her face with scientific seriousness. "Maybe you sleep on a dirty pillowcase."

"That was my first theory. I changed it. Didn't help." She grabbed two bottles and turned them over. "So now I'm reading labels, because labels have to tell you what's actually in there."

The first bottle said it fought oil. The second said it removed excess oil gently. She flipped to the back panels and found tiny words like salicylic acid and oil-free. Then, on a pamphlet tucked behind the shelf, she found a paragraph that made her stop dead. Hormones in puberty, it said, make the oil glands in the skin produce more oil, and that extra oil is called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.

"Sebum," she read aloud. "That's the actual word for it."

"So it's not my pillowcase theory," Maddox said.

"It's not dirt at all. It's me. My own skin started making extra oil because of puberty." She felt a strange, buzzing relief. The cause was invisible, but it had a name, and named things could be fought.

She picked the face wash that said oil-free, paid the cashier, and practically bounced out the door. Halfway home she spotted Ms. Berg on her porch, arguing on the phone with her landlord about a leaky pipe, and waved so hard she nearly dropped her bag. Ms. Berg covered the phone and mouthed, "Tomorrow?" Rebecca nodded. Tomorrow was Saturday, and Maddox and Caroline were coming over to build the model volcano for science class, the one they'd decided would accelerate baking soda and vinegar with a secret extra ingredient.

That night Rebecca washed her face exactly as the bottle directed, twice, and studied the three bumps in the mirror like a general studying enemy territory.

"Okay, sebum," she said. "I know your name now."

She snapped off the light and grinned at the dark.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Megan had claimed the window seat with a blanket, two granola bars, and a photocopied story called "The Scarlet Ibis" that Ms. Takahashi had handed out on Friday. Monday's assignment sat underlined twice at the top of the page: find the foreshadowing, find the symbolism, explain what each one suggests. Megan had read the first three pages at the kitchen table, where her little brother kept invading her space to ask if she knew where the tape was, so she had retreated to the nook and pulled the curtain half shut behind her.

The narrator's little brother, Doodle, was small and fragile and not supposed to live long, though he did. Megan got that far easily. Then, on page six, a red bird blew in with a storm and dropped out of the tree into the family garden, and the family crowded around it, and the bird died there among the flowers. Megan read the paragraph twice. A strange bird in a strange garden, red as blood, dying right in front of the fragile boy. She texted Emelia.

"Is a bird dying in the garden supposed to mean something or is it just a bird"

Emelia texted back fast, which meant she was also avoiding homework. "Ms. T said stories don't waste ink. If it feels too obvious it's on purpose."

Megan chewed her pen. Too obvious, maybe, or too ambiguous to prove. She flipped ahead to test the idea, since guessing was cheaper than rereading. At the end, the narrator ran through a storm, and Doodle, fragile Doodle, fell behind, and when the brother went back for him, Doodle was under a bush, and the narrator described him in a way that made Megan close the book for a second. A storm. Red. A fragile thing left out in the weather. The bird paragraph was doing the same job three pages early, the way erosion works, quiet and repeated, wearing the story down to one ending the whole time.

"So it was foreshadowing," Emelia said later on the phone. "The bird is Doodle. That's also the symbolism part, right? The red bird in the garden is literally foreshadowing Doodle dying."

"That's my whole paragraph," Megan said. "I wrote that a storm-blown red bird dies in the garden and it hints at what happens to the fragile boy later. Ms. Takahashi will either love it or think I copied something."

"You didn't?"

"I had two granola bars and a hunch. That's it."

On Monday, Ms. Takahashi handed the essays back and paused at Megan's desk. She tapped the margin beside one line, where she had written in green ink, "Yes. Exactly this." Megan slid the paper under her binder before Karter, sitting one seat over, could lean over and read it.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: To clear a fraction from an equation, multiply both sides by its denominator: if x divided by 3 equals 5, multiplying both sides by 3 gives x = 15.
story:
Nolan sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with his math notebook open and twenty minutes left before Grandpa's favorite show started, which meant the TV room was off limits until the dishes were done. Jayde and Riaan had biked over with him, and now all three of them stared at the same problem on the page: x divided by 3 equals 5.

"Five what," Riaan said, dropping into the chair beside him. "Just five?"

"That's the whole problem." Nolan tapped the paper. "Mr. Müller gave us this exact one yesterday and said it would be on Friday's quiz. I wasn't listening when he explained it. I was drawing a hawk."

Jayde pulled a granola bar from her bag, checked the label, and put it back. "Almonds. Your grandma's allergy is almonds, right? I'm not risking it in her kitchen." She leaned over the notebook instead. "Couldn't you just guess? Try a number."

Nolan had tried guessing last night, and it hadn't worked, and he'd shoved the notebook under his bed and played a game instead. He remembered that choice now, sitting here with Riaan watching him and the clock ticking toward five o'clock, when they all had to bike home before the streetlights came on. "Guessing didn't coincide with being right," he said. "I tried six. I tried eight. It's like throwing rocks at a window in the dark."

Outside the window, something rustled in the hedge, and Grandpa, drying a plate at the sink, said without turning around, "Hedgehog. Nocturnal little things, but they come out early when it's about to rain. Quick, before the dishes."

Nolan looked at the equation again. Divided by 3 equals 5. Then he thought about the three of them and the money question Jayde had asked on the ride over, about splitting fifteen dollars three ways, five each. He flipped his pencil over and erased his guesses.

"If each share is five dollars and there are three of us, the total has to be three fives. Fifteen." He wrote 3 beside the fraction bar, then another 3 on the other side of the equals sign. "So if I times this side by 3 to undo the dividing, I have to times the other side by 3 too, or it stops being equal." He worked it through, and there it was, plain as the rain starting to tap the window. "x equals 15."

"Try another one," Jayde said, spinning the notebook toward herself and writing x divided by 3 equals 5 in bigger letters, just to be annoying.

Riaan grinned. "Same one."

"That's the trick. Do it with no pencil."

Nolan set the pencil down anyway, folded his hands, and said, "Fifteen."

"Okay," Jayde admitted, "that's fast."

Grandpa stacked the last plate, and the theme music of his show started up in the other room. "Dishes are done. And Nolan," he said, pausing at the doorway, "keep the notebook out on the porch. Rain's good for thinking."

They carried the math to the porch swing, and Jayde said, "Now x divided by 3 equals 7, no pencil, go."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Edouard's sneakers squeaked on the community centre floor as he carried the last poster board toward the cultural festival booth. In twenty minutes, Ms. Cohen would walk through every display with her clipboard, and their table still had a blank spot where the caption card should go.

"Read it to me one more time," Isobel said, tape strips stuck to her sleeve like feathers.

Edouard held up his draft. "This drum was made by an Inuit artist from Iqaluit, and one Inuit told our class how it generates its deep sound when the hide is heated by fire." He frowned at his own handwriting. "Something about that is wrong."

Abel, who had spent the whole morning hauling folding chairs and now looked like he had used up a week of stamina in three hours, leaned over the card. "You wrote an Inuit twice. Doesn't that mean more than one person?"

"That's what I can't figure out," Edouard said. He turned the card over and over, as if the answer might be hiding on the back. He thought about French class, where he was Edouard to strangers but "Ti-Ed" to his grandmother, two names for the same boy. Maybe this was like that too. "I'll go ask. There's a woman at the throat-singing table who talked to our class."

He wove between the booths, past the smell of frybread and the sound of a steel drum, until he reached the singer adjusting her microphone. He explained his problem and held out the card.

She laughed kindly. "Inuit means 'the people.' One person is called an Inuk."

Edouard repeated it under his breath so he would not lose it on the walk back. "So it's 'an Inuk artist,' and 'one Inuk told our class.'" He slowed down. Inuktitut, the language she had named, echoed in his head. People who speak a language get to say who they are in it, he realized, the way his grandmother called herself Acadienne and never just Canadian.

Back at the table, Isobel had the tape ready and Abel had cleared a space, so all Edouard had to do was write. His hand shook a little, which surprised him, since a caption was only fourteen words. He felt weirdly vulnerable putting someone else's word on a public sign, and he checked each letter twice before he set down the pen.

Ms. Cohen arrived at 4:58, read the card, and tapped it with her clipboard. "Well done. This is exactly right."

The throat-singer passed their booth later, read the caption, and gave Edouard a thumbs-up. "Nice work," she called. "An Inuk appreciates it."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
story:
Eli sat on the curb outside the art cabin with his sketchbook balanced on his knees, glaring at his drawing of Main Street. Ms. Desir had shown them one-point perspective that morning: every line of the street, the rooftops, the sidewalk edges, had to run toward a single dot on the paper. She called it the vanishing point. His dot was there, his lines converged on it, and still the street looked wrong. Flat, somehow. Like it was being seen by nobody.

Drew plopped down beside him with his own sketchbook, having drawn the same street from the window of the mess hall upstairs. "Yours looks weird," Drew said, which was not helpful. Eli leaned over anyway. Drew's street felt high up, like looking down from a window, while Eli's felt low, like a kid's view from the curb. Same street, same lesson, same vanishing point trick, and yet the two drawings felt nothing alike.

Eli flipped back through his sketchbook to the drawing he'd made before lunch. The horizon line, the flat line where his dot sat, had been near the top of that page. On the current drawing he'd put it near the bottom without deciding to. He thought about a choice he'd made that morning, when he'd abandoned the porch steps and sat down on the curb instead because the steps were already colonized by the older campers sprawled across every inch of them. He had chosen the curb without thinking. He checked Drew's paper again: Drew's horizon line sat high on the page, and Drew had drawn from upstairs. The pattern held. A low horizon made a street feel seen from a child's height, and a high one from a window above.

He tested it right there. He drew the same street twice more, once with the horizon line low, once with it high, changing nothing else. The low one felt like standing on the sidewalk. The high one felt like leaning out a window. He held them up beside each other, heart beating faster than a drawing really deserved.

Ariel wandered over from the dock, dripping lake water, and studied all four drawings spread across the curb. "So which is the right one?" she asked.

"Both," Eli said. "Depends where you're standing." He picked up his pencil, turned to a fresh page, and drew his horizon line low, right where a twelve-year-old's eyes would be. "This one's mine."

"Verdict?" Drew asked, tapping the page.

"Durable," Eli said, and started on the rooftops.

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Charles Darwin published his theory of evolution by natural selection in the book On the Origin of Species in 1859.
story:
Nathaniel knelt in the community garden with a seed packet in one hand and a problem in his head. Ms. Hughes, who ran the garden club, had promised the last plot of the season to whoever brought in the best project for the science fair, and April had already claimed the topic of volcanoes. Kaydence wanted tornadoes. Nathaniel only had a crumpled worksheet about birds, which did not seem like much of anything.

At home that weekend, his grandfather took him to a second-hand bookshop to kill a rainy afternoon. Nathaniel wandered the narrow aisles while his grandfather chatted with the cashier, an old colleague from his bus-driving days. On a bottom shelf, wedged between cookbooks, Nathaniel found a battered green cover. On the Origin of Species, by Charles Darwin. He flipped to the title page, squinting at the faded print. "Grandpa, it says 1859. That's when he published it?" His grandfather leaned over, tapped the date with one finger, and said Darwin had been arguing about it ever since. Nathaniel checked the date twice, because Kaydence would ask, and Kaydence caught everything.

Back in the garden on Monday, he spread his worksheet on the potting bench. It showed finches from different islands, some with thick blunt beaks, some with long thin ones. Ms. Hughes had drawn a question mark beside them. Nathaniel thought about the seed packet in his pocket, the one with big hard sunflower seeds, and an idea began to form. He could test it. He filled one tray with big seeds, another with tiny poppy seeds, and handed chopsticks, tweezers, and pliers to whoever walked by. "Pretend the tool is your beak. Get as many seeds as you can in thirty seconds."

Kaydence, who was usually impulsive and grabbed the pliers without asking, crushed the poppy seeds and pouted. April, more careful, picked up the tweezers and cleaned out the tiny seeds before anyone else had started. With the big sunflower seeds, the pliers won easily and the tweezers barely managed three. Nathaniel wrote the numbers down so fast his pen tore the paper.

"The birds didn't choose their beaks," he said slowly, watching April refill the tray for a kid from the apartment block who had wandered in and wanted a turn. "The island chose for them. Whatever food was there, the beaks that matched it won." Nobody had intervened to change the birds; the islands had done it themselves, over a very long time, and a man in 1859 had figured out how to say so in a book.

Ms. Hughes came over with the watering can and looked at his chart. "So what happened on the islands with big seeds?" Nathaniel held up the pliers. "Finches like these. Want to try? April will time you."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
story:
The number 42 bus smelled like rain and vinyl seats, and Hannah was still turning the museum worksheet over in her hands when she sat down behind Mouhamed and Olive. The class had spent an hour at the World War II exhibit, and one display kept snagging in her mind: a wall of bright posters, bold slogans, smiling crowds. "Everyone is joining," one poster had said, though she couldn't remember joining what. Mr. Oyelaran had told them to look for how the posters tried to convince people, not what they said, and that instruction had started to irritate her, because the more she tried, the more posters she found doing it.

"Okay," she said, leaning over the seat in front of her. "That poster with the huge crowd. It didn't give one reason to join. It just said everybody already had." Mouhamed twisted around. "That's the bandwagon thing. My brother talks about it with sneaker ads. If everyone has them, you want them." Olive pulled out her phone and read from her notes: "Some of them used words like 'pure' and 'traitor.' Loaded words. They make you feel instead of think." The bus hissed to a stop, and three more students from the class climbed on, still arguing about the exhibit.

Hannah stared out the window, tracing it in her head. A poster used a famous athlete, and another one showed a film star. Testimonials, Olive had called them, when a famous face stands in for an argument. "It's like a machine," Hannah said slowly. "Bandwagon, loaded words, famous faces. All the pieces doing the same job." Mouhamed grinned. "That's a good metaphor. A persuasion machine." But a machine has a builder, and that thought stuck with her more than any poster.

Back at the museum, she had photographed the small label beside the display, and now she zoomed in on it. "In March 1933," she read aloud, "Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda." A whole ministry. A government office built to make those posters, and it was new, that same year, like it was one of the first things they set up. The persuasion machine wasn't an accident; somebody had designed it, on purpose, with a budget. She felt the hair on her arms rise, even on the warm bus.

"So all those tricks, the crowds, the words, the movie stars," Olive said, "someone sat in an office and chose them?" Hannah nodded. "A whole ministry of it." The bus lurched around a corner, and their worksheets slid to the floor in a heap. Mouhamed bent to grab them and came up holding an ad torn from a magazine, someone's leftover, showing a robust grinning soccer player holding a soda. "Look what just fell out of my backpack," he said, waving it. "Guess the machine's still running." Hannah took the ad from him and turned it over, looking for who had printed it.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: To ask for the bill in a Spanish-speaking restaurant, a customer can say "La cuenta, por favor," meaning "The bill, please."
story:
The restaurant smelled of garlic and fried potatoes, and every table was full. Amelia's dad kept checking his watch while her mom stacked the empty plates and pushed them to one side. The waiter had cleared their dinners twenty minutes ago and never come back.

"Maybe they forgot us," Dad muttered.

Amelia thought about that. The waiter hadn't forgotten them. He had swept past their table four times, once carrying a tray of coffees, once wiping the counter, and he had smiled at their table each time. A waiter who remembers you doesn't forget you. He was waiting for something, the same way the family at the next table had raised a hand and called out before their check appeared.

Flashback: back in Spanish class, Ms. Chanthavong had made them act out a café scene. Yasmin had played the waiter and refused to bring Amelia's imaginary check no matter how loudly she pointed at her empty plate. "You have to ask for it," Yasmin had whispered, grinning, and Maxx had scribbled something on a napkin and slid it across the desk. Amelia had copied it into her notebook without really reading it.

She dug the notebook out of her backpack now, right there at the table. There it was, in her own handwriting under a smudge of pencil: La cuenta, por favor.

She looked around the room. The owners were handing out menus from a stack they kept behind the register, distributing them to the two groups waiting at the door. The place was packed, and every check on every table meant more money coming in, but a table that sat empty and paid never was revenue for anyone. The waiter wasn't ignoring them. He just hadn't been asked.

Amelia stood up. Her mouth was dry and the words felt too big, but when the waiter passed with a stack of plates balanced on his arm, she said it. "La cuenta, por favor."

He stopped, shifted the plates, and nodded twice. "Ahora mismo." The words sounded distinct and quick, and she didn't know what they meant, but he turned straight toward the register, and a minute later a small tray arrived at their table with a printed slip of paper on it.

"That's it?" her mom said, staring at the check. "We've been sitting here for half an hour."

"He was waiting for us to ask," Amelia said, closing her notebook. "I had it in here the whole time."

Her dad counted out the euros and left the tip. Outside, the street was loud with scooters and café music. Amelia slid the notebook back into her pack, and Yasmin's voice from that classroom popped into her head, clear as a bell: "You have to ask for it."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
story:
The flyer taped to the library door promised five hundred dollars for the winner of the "Design an Ad" contest, and Zoe read it three times before her backpack strap slid off her shoulder. Five hundred dollars would cover the overdue fines on her account and the rest of what her mom had been saving toward the family trip to visit Grandma, the tropical postcard on the fridge the only sunshine in their kitchen that winter. She copied the rules into her notebook: make a persuasive poster for the library's new reading program, real techniques, judges looking for you to know your stuff.

She spread her materials across the table by the window, where the radiator ticked and smelled like dust. Rayyan dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of magazines he had pulled from the recycling bin, glossy pages of cereal boxes and soda ads. "Mr. Cardinal said to study real ads," he said, tearing one out. "Look, this one has a basketball player holding the drink. That's a celebrity testimonial." Zoe nodded. "And that gum ad says everyone's switching to it. Bandwagon." Baby arrived last, shaking rain off her jacket, and flopped down with a box of crackers she'd bought with her last dollar. On the front, in swirly green letters, it said "all-natural goodness."

"Natural goodness," Zoe said slowly. "What does that even mean, though?" She picked up the box, turned it over, and read the ingredient list out loud: things with nine syllables, three kinds of oil, a color additive. Baby's face fell. "I bought it because it sounded healthy." Zoe copied the phrase into her notebook, then flipped through the magazine pile and found the same trick everywhere. "Pure." "Classic." "Freedom to choose." None of the words said anything you could actually check, and they all felt warm, like the radiator.

When Mr. Cardinal passed by with his cart of returns, Zoe held up the cracker box. "Glittering generalities," she said. "Vague, nice-sounding words, like 'natural' or 'freedom,' that make you feel good without saying anything specific you could look up." He tapped the box twice and kept walking, and Zoe grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. Her poster almost drew itself after that: a shining, empty box labeled with beautiful words, and beside it, the honest little ingredient list nobody read. When the winners were posted two weeks later, her name was second. Second place was a fifty-dollar gift card, not the five hundred, and the trip fund stayed short, and Baby never did get her dollar back. Zoe clipped the certificate to the fridge next to the tropical postcard, and stood there looking at both of them while the rain on the window made the beach in the picture seem to evaporate.

"At least now I can't be fooled," Baby said behind her.

"Want some crackers?" Zoe asked, holding out the box.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: In Excel, a 'bar chart' has horizontal bars and a 'column chart' has vertical bars, although both compare amounts across categories.
story:
Juliette had exactly forty minutes of computer lab to prove that her family's movie nights were out of control. She had tracked every movie they had watched since September in her notebook: eleven comedies, four horror movies, two documentaries, and one musical that her dad had fallen asleep during. Her plan was to put it all in a spreadsheet, add up the counts with a formula, and turn it into a chart for her presentation on Friday.

She opened the file and typed her categories down column A, one genre per row. Comedy, horror, documentary, musical. Then the counts next to each one in column B. In the cell below the numbers she typed =SUM(B2:B5), and when she pressed Enter the number 18 appeared, which meant her formula had worked, and also that eighteen movies since September was possibly too many movies. She saved the file twice, because she was not a fool.

The chart was where things went sideways, literally. She clicked Insert, picked the first chart the menu offered her, and the whole thing came out lying down. Her comedy bar, which should have stood tall and proud at eleven, stretched sideways across the screen like it was napping. Denver leaned over from the next computer.

"Your chart's asleep," he said.

"It's not asleep, it's horizontal." Juliette stared at it. The bars were all there, the right lengths, the right categories, just tipped over on their sides. So the data was fine. That meant the problem wasn't in her numbers, it was in the type of chart she'd picked. She tried to diagnose it the way Mr. Yoon kept telling them to, by looking at what was actually there instead of what she'd assumed. The menu had said bar chart. She had wanted bars going up.

She clicked back into the menu and read the options properly this time. Column chart. She picked it, and her chart stood up straight, four tidy towers, comedy towering over everything at eleven. Annie wandered over and pointed at the screen. "So what's the difference?"

"Bars go sideways, columns go up," Juliette said. "Even though they show the same thing."

"Huh," said Annie, and went back to her own computer, where her chart was also, Juliette now noticed, lying down. Juliette raised her hand and called across the lab, "Annie. Check your chart type." She decided not to mention it to Denver, whose spreadsheet appeared to consist entirely of one column that said "snacks" forty times. That was a different problem, and nobody could fix it in forty minutes.

When the bell rang, she printed her chart, upright and assertive, comedy bar at the top like a flag planted on a hill. She slid it into her binder and carried it out under her arm.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee.
story:
The community center gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn. Addison sat in the third row of folding chairs with fourteen other spellers, her number pinned to her shirt, and watched the pronouncer shuffle his cards. In the first round, Magalie went out on "rhinoceros," missing the h. In the second round, Lucie got "tsunami" and spelled it slowly, letter by letter, and survived.

Addison's word was "compress." She asked for the definition, then for it in a sentence, and the pronouncer said, "You can compress a sponge by squeezing it." She spelled it and sat down, her heart loud in her ears. Two rounds later, only five spellers were left.

Here was her problem. Every time she stood at the microphone, the letters she had studied on her flashcards seemed to scatter, as though some unseen hand had reached into her memory and shaken it. She could not see the cause, so she had started watching for one. At the community center's little library, where she studied every Tuesday, she had noticed something else, and it had given her an idea.

She had been flipping through a book about spelling bee champions when she found a page about recent winners. "In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee," she had read out loud to Lucie, who was copying words onto index cards across the table. Addison had copied the name onto a card of her own and tacked it above her desk at home. Now, waiting for her turn, she pressed her thumbnail into her palm and thought about that card. Zaila Avant-garde had also had to keep her letters in order under the lights, in front of everyone. Addison decided that the letters were probably not scattering on their own. They scattered because she rushed, because she started spelling before she had finished hearing the word.

So she tested it. When the pronouncer gave her "robust," she did not begin at once. She said, "Definition, please." He said, "Strong and sturdy." She said, "Language of origin?" He said, "Latin." Only then did she spell, at the speed she used at her desk, unhurried, one letter arriving after the last. "R-O-B-U-S-T. Robust." The bell stayed silent, and she walked back to her chair.

The final word came down to Addison and a boy from another school. The pronouncer said, "Momentum." She asked for the sentence. "The sled gained momentum going down the hill." She let the whole word settle in her head, took one breath, and spelled it the way she wrote it, left to right, no gaps.

"Correct," the judge said. "We have a winner." Addison looked over at Magalie and Lucie, who were both standing up and waving their arms, and she pressed her thumb one last time into her palm.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Herman Snellen developed his eye chart of rows of shrinking letters in 1862.
story:
Abigail had been hiding her new glasses in her backpack for two days, and Priya was getting suspicious. "You either wear them or I wear them," Priya announced on Saturday, sprawled on Abigail's bedroom floor. "Those purple frames would look incredible on me, and you know it."

"They'd look incredible on me too," Abigail said. "That's not the problem." The problem was that everyone at school would see her, and she wasn't sure the glasses even worked. The eye exam had been quick and strange: cover one eye, read the letters, cover the other. Then a machine had puffed air at her eyeballs, which she considered a personal attack.

She pulled a folded paper out of her desk and smoothed it flat. "The nurse gave me this. It's a copy of the chart she used." Rows of letters marched down the page, each row smaller than the one above. Priya leaned in and squinted at the bottom row, which was mostly a rumor. "Who invented this thing? It's diabolical."

"Diabolical and diagonal," Abigail said, tilting the paper. "Half of these letters are slanted on purpose, I swear." At the bottom, in small print, she found the answer to Priya's question and read it out loud. "Herman Snellen developed this eye chart in 1862."

Priya sat up so fast she knocked over a marker. "Wait. Eighteen sixty-two? That's older than anyone's great-grandparents. Every single person who has ever failed the bottom row of this thing has been squinting at Herman Snellen's letters for more than a hundred and fifty years." She flopped back down, delighted. "That man has been personally embarrassing kids since before electricity."

Abigail taped the chart to her closet door, ignoring Priya's commentary about Herman judging them from beyond. She stepped back to the far end of the room, which was about the distance from the nurse's chair to her wall, more or less. "I'm going to simulate the exam," she said. "If I can read the same row I failed at school, then the glasses work, and I've been hiding them for no reason. If I can't, I march back to the eye doctor." She pushed the purple frames onto her face.

The room changed. The poster on her wall, which she had assumed was an impressionist blur, turned out to be a sailboat. The bottom row of the chart snapped into letters, sharp and slightly smug. "E, F, P, T, O, Z," she read, then read it again just to feel the phenomenon repeat itself. "Priya. There's a spider on your shoulder."

Priya screamed and slapped at her own arm. Abigail laughed so hard the glasses slid down her nose. There was no spider, of course, but that was the whole point: now she could tell the difference. "Monday," she said, wiping her eyes. "I'm wearing them Monday. And I'm telling everyone Herman Snellen made me do it."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Natural selection requires three things: individuals that vary, traits that are inherited, and some variations helping individuals survive and reproduce more than others.
story:
Arthur stood at the picnic table in his backyard with six spoons, a bag of sunflower seeds, and a pair of chopsticks he had borrowed from the kitchen drawer without asking. His science test was on Friday, and the question he feared most was the one about the finches on the islands, the ones whose beaks changed over time. He understood the birds in pictures, but every time he tried to explain them out loud, the words slid away from him like water off a slide.

"You're going to stab yourself with those," Blanche said, climbing over the back fence the way she always did, like the gate did not apply to her. Serenity came through the gate properly, carrying a notebook.

"I'm doing an experiment," Arthur said. "Each tool is a different beak. The spoons are big wide beaks, the chopsticks are thin pointed ones, and these tweezers are somewhere in between. Whoever grabs the most seeds in thirty seconds wins."

"That's the most competitive thing you've ever invented," Serenity said, and she was already picking up a spoon.

They ran three rounds. Blanche swept the seeds into a pile with the spoon and dominated every time. The chopsticks kept dropping single seeds before they reached the cup. "Okay," Arthur said, panting a little, "so on the seed island, wide beaks win. That's the whole thing, right? Beaks change because the good ones win. Natural selection. Done. I can go inside now."

"Hold on," Serenity said, flipping to a fresh page. "You're missing pieces. My cousin made this mistake on her test. Imagine one seed island and one flower island, like nectar, deep flowers." She held up a tall cup of juice with a straw. "Thin beaks win here. But that's still not the whole story, or every bird everywhere would already have the perfect beak."

Arthur sat down on the bench, thinking hard enough that he forgot to defend his seeds from Blanche. "So the first thing is variation, right? Like how my spoon and my chopsticks are different. On a real island, the baby birds aren't identical." He lined up the tools in a row. "Then the beak shape has to be inherited, or the winners' advantage dies with them. A spoon champion has to make more spoon-shaped kids, or nothing changes down the line."

"And the third thing," Serenity said, tapping her pen, "is that some variations have to help more than others. Not just be different. Different and better, at surviving and having babies, on that particular island." Blanche demonstrated by sweeping the last seeds into her hand and grinning, which made the point better than any diagram.

Arthur tried his explanation out loud one more time, using the three conditions like a checklist, and this time it held together. "Variation, inherited, and some variations winning. All three, or it isn't natural selection." Ms. Fischer, his neighbor, called over the fence that if he was going to participate in outdoor shouting, could he at least keep the word "democracy" out of it, since Blanche had apparently been shouting about seed distribution being unfair. Arthur raised the tweezers, which had won nothing all afternoon, and declared them the neutral party in the dispute.

Blanche laughed and dumped all the seeds back into the bag for one final round, winner takes the whole bowl. Serenity set the timer, Arthur crouched over the cup of juice with his chopsticks, and somewhere over the fence a real bird was working at the feeder with a beak perfectly shaped for the job. "Ready," Serenity said. "Go."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
The lobby smelled like nothing, because it wasn't a real place, but Sadie swore she could feel the hum of it anyway, the way the servers somewhere ticked and blinked. Her headset crackled. Charlie-Rose's voice came through, tinny and urgent. "Sadie, did you check your email? Lilah says she didn't get your party invite, and now she thinks you left her out on purpose."

"I sent it to the whole class list," Sadie said. Her avatar, a lanky knight with a crooked helmet, stood in the stone plaza where players gathered before matches. She opened her email on the second screen while her knight waited. Sure enough, Lilah's name wasn't on the message she'd sent. Her heart dropped. Lilah had sat with her every day at lunch since the incident with the burned lasagna, and now she thought she'd been cut from a birthday party she'd helped plan.

"Wait," said a new voice. Ms. Visser, their eccentric neighbour, played the same game under the name Windrow99, and she was always turning up in the lobby at odd hours with her tea. "Check the field you used, dear. The one below CC."

Sadie scrolled. Last week, when she'd asked her dad about sending to thirty people at once, she'd found the answer herself by typing the letters into the help bar: BCC stands for blind carbon copy. People added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses. That was why she'd used it, so nobody in the class got everybody's address. But now, staring at the sent message, she saw the problem. The class list had pasted into CC, not BCC. She must have clicked the wrong box.

Her mouse hovered. If she resent the invitation with Lilah's address added to the visible field, the whole class would see Lilah's address too, and Lilah's mother had once said, in no uncertain terms, that a plague of forwarded chain letters had followed one leaked address around for a year. Sadie couldn't embarrass Lilah like that. So she opened a fresh message, typed the invitation again, put the class list carefully into BCC this time, checked it twice, and added Lilah at the top. Then she called her through the headset, and Lilah picked up on the first ring.

"I thought you uninvited me because of the cake fight," Lilah said.

"There wasn't a cake fight. There was a cake incident, and it was Charlie-Rose's elbow."

"I know," Lilah said, and Sadie could hear her grinning. "I was testing whether you'd chase me down or let me sulk."

Sadie's knight finally got pulled into a match, a capture-the-flag round in a jungle map that smelled, she imagined, of wet leaves. She and Lilah and Charlie-Rose fought back to back and lost spectacularly anyway. Afterward, in the quiet plaza, Ms. Visser's voice drifted through the headset. "By the way, Sadie, the reason Lilah didn't get the first message is that her family changed email addresses last month. She's had the new one since before you sent anything."

Sadie looked at her sent folder, where her careful BCC sat hiding thirty addresses, and then at the second invitation she'd typed in a panic for no reason at all. "So the CC copy would have gone to a dead address anyway?"

"An address nobody answers," said Ms. Visser, sipping something that slurped audibly through the mic. "Lilah only checked the old account because Charlie-Rose told her to. Sent from the new one, of course."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
story:
Megan carried the last box up to apartment 4C and set it down on a floor so bare it looked barren, like the moving truck had scraped up even the dust. In her old building, Otis would have appeared in the hallway within minutes, pretending he'd come to borrow a whisk. Here, the hallway just smelled like someone else's dinner. She missed her friends the way you miss a sock in the laundry, constantly and in a specific shape, and she wanted one thing before school started tomorrow: proof that she wasn't just going to feel terrible forever.

Ms. Adebayo, the counselor at her new school, had given her a photocopied page at registration, saying only, "Read it when you get a chance, not before bed." Megan had read it before bed anyway. It was about a list from 1967, put together by two researchers named Holmes and Rahe, that scored life events by how much readjustment they demanded. She'd folded the page into her back pocket, where it had gone soft as a napkin, because one line had snagged in her head: both changing residence and changing schools were on the list. Not just one. Both. She had done both in a single August.

The problem was that a photocopied page couldn't be checked against reality by sitting on a bedroom floor, so Megan designed what she privately called an experiment and what her dad would have called pestering the neighbors. Her hypothesis: if the list was a real database of human experience and not just paper noise, then other people in this building who had moved should show the same wobbly symptoms she did. Symptom one: eating cereal for dinner because the pots were unpacked. Symptom two: calling the new corner store by the old neighborhood store's name. Symptom three, the big one: feeling off without being able to say off about what.

She started with the boy across the hall, who introduced himself as Brantley and immediately tried to regulate the situation by offering her half a popsicle, because in his view no conversation should be conducted empty-handed. His family had moved in three weeks ago, from two floors down. "Same building, different floor," Megan said, pencil ready. "Did it still count?" Brantley thought hard, popsicle dripping. "I called my own room the wrong name for four days," he said. "I'd walk in and think, this isn't my room, and then remember it was." She wrote it down.

By evening she had interviewed a family on the fifth floor who still ordered pizza from their old town out of loyalty, and a woman on two who said moving had "scrambled her soup," which Megan recorded as a technical term. Every single mover had symptoms. The list held up. Feeling off after a move wasn't a personal defect, it was practically a documented law, with her whole building as evidence.

The next morning Megan stood outside her new classroom, and when Brantley slid up beside her with two popsicles, she took one. "Holmes and Rahe," she said, tapping her pocket. "Look them up, it's a whole list." Brantley saluted with his popsicle, and they walked in together.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Blushing happens when blood vessels in the face widen and let more blood flow near the skin.
story:
Willow had rehearsed three jokes on the walk to the stadium, and now, standing in line for hot chocolate with Simone, she couldn't remember any of them. Her date, a boy from science class, was already at the gate, holding two tickets and pretending very hard that he wasn't looking for her.

"You're doing the thing where you breathe like a dragon," Simone said. "Stop it."

"I'm fine. It's just a football game." But it wasn't just a football game, and Simone knew it, because Willow had talked about nothing else for four days. The plan was simple: meet at the gate, sit together on the bleachers, share the nachos Willow's mom had given her money for. Nutritious, her mom had said, was not the word for stadium nachos, but she'd handed over the five dollars anyway.

The first quarter went well. The home team scored, everyone stood up and yelled, and Willow discovered that shouting next to someone made it easier to talk to them. By the second quarter she had remembered her joke about the biology textbook, and when she told it, he laughed so hard he nearly knocked his drink over. Then Simone, sitting one row back, leaned forward and whispered, "Willow. Your face. You're turning red."

Willow snatched her phone and used the dark screen like a mirror. Simone was right. Her cheeks were pink all the way up to her ears. "Make it stop," she whispered.

"You can't just make it stop," Simone said. "Blushing happens when blood vessels in your face widen and let more blood flow near the skin." She said it matter-of-factly, like she was reading a homework question, then shrugged. "Everybody does it."

Willow looked at her reflection again and thought about that. If the blood was coming up near the skin, that meant the pink would be right there where she could watch it, not hiding somewhere. So she tested it. She held the phone up, picked a spot on her cheek, and counted quietly while the crowd chanted for the kickoff. Twenty seconds, thirty. The pink didn't vanish, but it faded, seeping back down like water drying off a window, exactly the way blood retreating from the skin ought to look. It followed a rule, and rules, Willow had always felt, were better than surprises.

She put the phone away. The boy turned to her, still grinning about the joke, and asked if she had any more like that.

"One," Willow said. "But you have to wait until my face is my regular color, or you'll miss the punchline." He laughed again, and this time she just let the warmth climb her cheeks, because now she knew where it was going and how it left.

"Okay," she said. "Ready."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A timekeeper watches how long each agenda item takes, so one topic does not use up the time planned for the others.
story:
Mila counted the minutes on the classroom clock as Ms. Lin gathered her papers and left the room. The Robot Club had done it again. Three meetings in a row, they had never reached the last item on the agenda, the one about the fundraiser, because the argument about wheel types ate everything. Tonight she spread the agenda on the desk before anyone arrived and wrote numbers beside each item, ten minutes for wheels, five for the field trip, ten for the fundraiser.

"A timekeeper," she announced when Jaxxon and Pyper dropped into their seats. "We need one. A timekeeper watches how long each agenda item takes, so one topic doesn't use up the time planned for the others." Jaxxon rolled his eyes, but Pyper, who loved stopping watches during track practice, volunteered on the spot.

The meeting started rough. Jaxxon launched into a speech about treads versus wheels, and Pyper called time at the ten-minute mark even though Jaxxon was mid-sentence. He slumped and muttered that the whole thing was pointless if nobody got to finish a thought. Mila felt the same worry. Why did cutting him off make the meeting worse instead of better?

She thought about it while Pyper reset the timer. The problem wasn't the timer, she decided. It was that Jaxxon never knew the end was coming. "What if we say 'two minutes left' before the timer goes off?" she asked. That was her test, and Jaxxon sat up straighter when she said it. It was like the timer became a signal they could all see coming instead of a trapdoor.

The next item, the field trip, went better. They collaborated on the permission slip wording, and when Pyper said "two minutes left," they wrapped up their ideas without anyone getting cut in half. Mila noticed a pattern forming: warnings, then endings, then smooth transitions. Her mind felt fertile with other plans, a parking lot list for ideas that didn't fit their item, a percentage of time reserved for open talk at the very end.

They reached the fundraiser with four minutes to spare. Pyper read out the total from the timer sheet, and Jaxxon, who had argued hardest about wheels, actually smiled. "We got through everything," he said. "Next week I'll take a turn as timekeeper." Mila wrote that at the top of next week's agenda, then drew a small clock beside it and slid the paper into her binder.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
story:
Evan had a race number safety-pinned to the back of his shorts, which was odd, because he was standing in his own backyard. On the back of the number, in pencil, he had written "3:00" and under it "90, 90." Morgan sat on the picnic table with a stopwatch and a bag of chips, and Morgan had her own plan: she was making a video for the school's morning announcements, and she wanted it to have at least one moment where somebody did something heroic.

"You can't be heroic in a backyard," Evan said.

"Watch me," said Morgan. "Lap one."

The trouble was the backyard. It held maybe forty metres of fence-to-fence grass, so Evan had made a loop around the picnic table, the shed, and the dead birch at the corner. He figured twelve loops for each "lap," and the math on the race number was the part he actually trusted. His coach had said the goal for the spring meet was three minutes for eight hundred metres, and the track was four hundred metres around, so Evan had sat at his desk the night before and worked it out. To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap. Two laps. Ninety seconds each. It felt almost insultingly simple, which was exactly why he suspected it wasn't.

The first time he tried it, he sprinted the whole first lap because sprinting felt like trying, and Morgan clicked the watch at 68 seconds. "That's heroic," she said. By the second lap his legs had gone soft, like the spine of a very old book, and he finished in 3:24, which was not. The second time, he jogged the first lap, came through in 102, and finished in 3:31, somehow worse. He lay on the grass with his arms out, staring at the birch.

"The problem is invisible," he said to the sky. "I can't see the pace. I just feel fast or slow, and my feelings are basically obsolete." Morgan offered him a chip, which he took. Then he had the idea. "Don't tell me the time until halfway. Just say 'good' if I'm near ninety and 'slow' if I'm under. One word."

He ran again. Around the table, past the shed, under the birch, twelve loops, and somewhere in there Morgan called "good," once, quietly. He crossed the line at 3:01, close enough that he stood with his hands on his knees and laughed at the grass. Morgan stopped the video and looked at her screen with the expression of someone who has just been given exactly what she wanted.

"Thirty seconds before the end, you stopped watching your feet," she said. "You looked up at the corner. I got that part."

"Did I look heroic?"

"Let's find out." She hit play.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The first three weeks of the season were a disaster, and Aurora was keeping notes. Every Tuesday and Thursday at the Riverside Community Center, the new floor hockey team found a fresh way to fall apart. Desmond insisted on playing defense even when the coach put him at forward. Aikam wouldn't pass to anyone who hadn't earned it, which so far meant nobody. Last practice, two boys on the team had shoved each other into the bleachers over a dropped pass, and Aurora had gone home with her jaw tight.

She lay on her bedroom floor that night with her notebook open. Something was wrong with the team, but not the obvious something. It wasn't lack of skill; Aikam could dangle around three defenders. It wasn't effort, either. The arguing itself was the strange part. Players on brand-new teams fought like this, and then, sometimes, they stopped. Aurora wrote a question at the top of the page: is there a pattern to when teams click, or is it just luck?

At school the next day she typed her question into the library computer and scrolled past homework help sites until one result caught her eye. She read it twice, then copied it into her notebook word for word. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. She looked at the four words for a long moment. Forming, when a group is new and polite. Storming. Her whole team was living inside the second word.

That would have been good news, except for one thing. She couldn't see the stages happening, not the way she could see a bad pass or a selfish shot. If the storming phase was real and invisible, how would she know when it was ending? She decided to test it. Her simple idea: stop keeping score of the arguments and start keeping score of the moments when somebody did something for a teammate instead of themselves. If Tuckman was right, those moments should increase.

"Can I tell you guys a hypothetical?" she said at Thursday's practice, pulling Desmond and Aikam onto the stage side of the gym. "Hypothetically, if the three of us ran a give-and-go every single time down the floor, even when it doesn't work, what happens?" Aikam shrugged. Desmond frowned. "Then we're predictable," he said. "Or we're a unit," said Aurora. "It's a hypothetical, so we can't lose by testing it."

The give-and-go failed the first four times. On the fifth, Desmond faked the pass and Aikam still moved, dragging a defender with him, and the lane opened for the goal. Nobody cheered louder than Aikam, which surprised everyone including Aikam. After practice, he lingered by the stick rack. "I have to confess something," he said. "I stopped passing because I thought none of you cared if we won. I thought I was the only one." Desmond laughed and told an anecdote about his older brother's soccer team, how they'd screamed at each other all season and then won the league final. Nobody had known why it turned around, his brother said. It just had.

Aurora kept counting anyway, because her notebook was filling up with tally marks and the tally marks were climbing. In week six, the team stopped arguing about positions and started arguing about plays, which felt different, sharper, almost friendly. In week seven, they won their first game.

In week eight, Ms. Clarke, who ran the community center, stood at the gym door with her clipboard and shook her head at the score. "You know," she said, "I only gave you kids the Thursday slot because nobody else wanted it."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Motion sickness happens when the eyes and the balance organs in the inner ear send the brain conflicting signals about whether the body is moving.
story:
Carson slumped into the plastic chair at gate B14 with his bag of cheese crackers and his new paperback, and his stomach was already complaining, which seemed unfair because the plane hadn't even left yet. The drive to the airport had been the worst part. Two hours of winding highway, and he'd made the mistake of reading the whole way. His dad had said, "You always do this to yourself," but that didn't seem like an answer. Carson wanted to know why reading made him sick when just sitting in the car didn't.

At the next seat over, Quinton was building a tower out of luggage tags, and beyond him Yousif was arguing with his little sister about who got the window seat. Their teacher Ms. Nasser was on the same flight, heading to the same science conference as Carson's mom, and she looked up from her crossword. "Green around the gills, Carson?"

"Motion sickness," Carson said. "From reading in the car. But I don't get why reading makes it worse."

Ms. Nasher tapped her pen against her knee. "Your eyes and your ears are telling your brain two different stories," she said, and went back to her puzzle.

Carson chewed on that. His ears? He'd never thought about his ears being involved in a moving car at all. But there was that dizzy, tipping feeling on the curves, the sense that his body knew it was swaying even when he wasn't looking out the window. So his ears, or something in them, tracked movement. And his eyes, glued to a page in his lap, reported that the words were sitting still, which meant his body was sitting still. Two different stories. His brain got both at once and apparently handled it by making him want to throw up.

He turned to Quinton. "I want to test something. On the plane, I'll read for ten minutes, then look out the window for ten minutes. If my theory is right, one should be worse."

"You're going to replicate being carsick on purpose?" Quinton said. "On purpose?"

"Science," Carson said, though the smell of the cheese crackers was already questionable.

Yousif wandered over. "My sister says only little kids get carsick. Like it's a baby thing."

"That's just a stereotype," Carson said. "It happens to pilots and stuff. It's about signals, not age."

When they boarded, Carson took the middle seat between his mom and the window, because Yousif's sister had claimed hers and there was no use fighting. He set a timer on his watch. For the first ten minutes he read, and the moment the plane taxied and turned, his stomach began its slow, familiar roll, like a tide coming in. The letters seemed to float on the page. Then he put the book down, leaned across his mom, and stared hard out the window at the runway sliding past, the terminal, the other planes. Now his eyes saw movement and whatever lived in his ears felt movement, and the two stories matched. The rolling in his stomach backed off, not instantly, but like a wave going out again.

"Huh," he said out loud.

"Feeling better?" his mom asked.

"Yeah. The window seat is medicine." He watched the runway lights blur as they picked up speed, and he decided he would spend takeoff looking nowhere else.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
Gabriel stood behind the registration table in the library's community room, word list folded in his back pocket, and watched the clock above the biography shelves tick toward two o'clock. The county spelling bee started in twenty minutes, and his hands would not stay still.

"You look like you're going to be sick," said Laurie, bouncing on her heels beside him. "You studied that list all week. Rereading it for the tenth time won't help now."

"That's the problem," Gabriel said. "I've reread it so many times the words feel familiar, but familiar isn't the same as knowing. Last night I closed the list and tried to write out page three, and I got maybe half."

Ludovic wandered over with a granola bar. "So what are you going to do, read it an eleventh time in nineteen minutes?"

Gabriel pulled Laurie's notebook out of her backpack before she could object. He handed her his list. "Quiz me. Don't show me anything. Just say the words and I spell them out loud, and mark the ones I miss." He had tried this on Tuesday with his dad, and the words he'd missed that night were the ones he still knew cold on Thursday. Getting it wrong first, somehow, made it stick.

He didn't have a reason for it until Mr. Sandhu, the librarian setting up the microphone, paused beside them. "That's the smart way," Mr. Sandhu said. "A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it."

"Really?" Gabriel said. "There's a whole study?"

"A whole study," Mr. Sandhu confirmed, and went back to untangling the microphone cord.

"Fine," Laurie said, opening the list. "Inherit."

"I-n-h-e-r-i-t," Gabriel said. His grandmother had inherited the farm, so the letters came easy. "Inflation. I-n-f-l-a-t-i-o-n. Money buys less when prices go up." He'd looked that one up himself after hearing it on the news.

"Molten," Laurie read.

"M-o-l-t-e-n." He saw the orange pour of lava in his mind. Then she said "vermilion," and he blanked. He tried again and got it wrong twice before she showed him: e before i, after the m. He spelled it four more times with his eyes shut, each time pulling it up from nothing instead of from the page.

"Spellers, take your seats," the judge announced.

Gabriel handed back the list and walked to the front row. Round three came the word "vermilion." His mouth was dry, but his hand was already moving, one letter at a time, like the word was rising up on its own.

"Correct," the judge said, and Laurie pumped her fist from the third row.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
Isabelle sat at the kitchen table with her flute, the recital program folded in front of her like a small white threat. Three days. Catherine had already texted twice asking if Isabelle had practiced the hard run in the second movement, and Isabelle had answered "yes" both times, which was true exactly once.

Her hands had been shaking all week. Her stomach hurt before school, and at night she lay awake listening to the radiator tick. She had looked up what was happening to her, half expecting something dramatic, and instead she found a plain sentence on a health website: stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can actually help a person focus, like before a test or a race. She read it twice. She'd been treating her nerves like a broken thing, something to hide, and the idea that they might be working for her felt like finding out a door she'd been pushing was a pull.

She decided to test it. That evening she practiced the second movement in the living room, where her little brother was building a tower of blocks and her mother was cooking something loud. Instead of trying to calm herself down first, she paid attention to what the jittery feeling did. Her eyes caught the sixteenth notes faster. When the run came, her fingers knew where to go before she thought about it. She played it clean, twice in a row, while spaghetti hissed on the stove.

"Since when can you do that?" her mother said, turning around with a wooden spoon.

"Since I stopped fighting it, maybe." Isabelle laughed, a real one, and texted Catherine: shaky hands are apparently useful, come over Saturday?

Catherine and Isha arrived the next afternoon with chips and their own panic. Isha was performing a piano piece and had been monitoring her worry levels all week on a phone app, which mostly made her more worried. "My mom says I need to learn boundaries," Catherine said, flopping onto the couch. "She means I should tell my violin teacher I can't do three extra lessons before the recital."

"You should tell her," Isabelle said. "That's not even about the recital, that's just too much." She told them what she had found, and what she had noticed in her own hands. Isha sat up straighter. "So it's like a short burst, not a permanent condition?" She tried her piece right there on Isabelle's upright piano, hands trembling, and the first page came out sharper than it had all week. "Okay," Isha said slowly. "Okay. That's different."

On Saturday afternoon Isabelle stood in the wings with Catherine, both of them shaking, the recital now inevitable and only twenty minutes away. Isabelle didn't try to stop the trembling this time. She let it climb her arms and waited, flute cold in her hands, listening for her name.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion.
story:
Riley spread the printouts across the lab bench, six product reviews for the same headphones, each one highlighted in a different color. His group had to sort every sentence into two piles, and Charles-Etienne had already put almost everything in the "facts" pile, including "These are the best headphones ever made."

"We're going to fail," Avah said, tapping that sentence. "Ms. López said one pile is stuff you can check and the other pile isn't. How do you check best?"

Charles-Etienne shrugged. "You look it up. Somebody tested them."

"Tested what, though? Loudness? Price?" Avah pulled the sheet back. "There's a difference between that and something like 'the battery lasts twenty hours.' You could time that."

Riley read down his own copy without saying anything. The coach's poster in the gym listed the Ming dynasty as the greatest in history, and that had bugged him for a week, because who decided? He started noticing that the sentences bothering him all carried the same kind of word. He picked up the yellow highlighter and marked "best" in the first review. Then "worst" in the third, where a reviewer called the case "the worst design I've seen." Then "beautiful," then "boring," then "should," twice.

"What are you doing?" Charles-Etienne asked.

"Every sentence I can't check has one of these words in it." Riley laid the sheets side by side. "Best, worst, beautiful, boring, should. The sentence right after them says the cord is one meter long. That one you could measure."

Avah leaned over. "Try it on the rest."

Riley went through all six reviews. Sentence by sentence, the pattern held. "The ear cushions are soft" went to opinion, because of nothing he could point to except that soft was a judgment, like the others. "The headphones cost ninety dollars" went to the check pile. "They should include a case" went to opinion, and he underlined should twice.

"So the words kind of symbolize something," he said, capping the highlighter. "When you see one, the whole sentence is probably a judgment, not a measurement."

"Great," Charles-Etienne said. "Then we're done. Almost everything is opinion."

"Then that's our project," Avah said. "Five reviews out of six are mostly judgment words. That's a finding. That's checkable, even."

Ms. López walked past their bench on her way to the aquarium. "Riley, is your group's sorting finished?"

"Almost. Can I borrow the meter stick from the supply cabinet?"

She glanced at the highlighted pages. "What for?"

"We want to see if the cord is actually one meter. If it isn't, that's a real error, not just somebody's opinion." He held up the review with the yellow marks. "Everything else on this page, we can't test. But this one line, we can."

Charles-Etienne was already unwinding the cord across the bench. Avah pinned one end down with her thumb, and Riley stretched the tape from zero.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
story:
Ava stood in her grandmother's kitchen with the last box of teacups, and the paper in her hand still said nothing but her name. Tomorrow she had to speak at the funeral. Her mother had asked her that morning, and the word she'd used was "eulogy," which Ava had looked up on her phone while the toast was burning. A eulogy was a speech praising a person who had died, from Greek roots meaning to speak well of. Speak well of. She kept turning the phrase over, because there was too much to say and only three minutes to say it.

Madison came through the back door without knocking, the way she always did, and set a grocery bag of cookies on the counter. "You're staring at a blank page," she said. "That's bad, right?"

"It's due tomorrow." Ava pulled two mugs from the box, and the smell of the cupboard, old cardboard and lavender, rose up so strong that she had to stop for a second. "The problem is I have to pick one memory. Just one. Three minutes, Mom says. So everything else gets excluded, like it didn't happen."

"So pick the best one," Madison said, as if that were simple.

But Ava had been trying all afternoon, and she had begun to notice a pattern in her memories, one she couldn't see directly but could test. When she tried to think of the "best" ones, the big ones, they came out flat in her head. The trip to the lake, the birthday when Grandma had arranged for a whole bakery cake shaped like a violin: when she rehearsed those out loud in the kitchen, they sounded like a commercial. When she let her mind wander instead, small things surfaced on their own. Grandma licking cake batter off her thumb while insisting the batter was for quality control. Grandma arguing with the insurance corporation on the phone for an hour about a ten-dollar charge, and winning.

Ava tested the idea out loud. She said the lake memory to Madison, then the batter one. "The second one sounded like her," Madison said. "The first one sounded like a yearbook caption."

"The big ones are for everybody," Ava said slowly, writing now. "The small ones are only for people who were actually there. That's why they're more, I don't know, authentic."

Ms. Smith, the neighbour, knocked and came in with a casserole dish, and when she heard what Ava was writing she said, "Your grandmother spoke at her own sister's funeral, you know. She talked for ten minutes about a bad haircut they gave each other in 1961." She laughed, then her eyes went wet, and she set the dish down carefully on the counter.

So Ava wrote the batter memory, and the insurance call, and the haircut story secondhand, and she read it aloud once in the kitchen while Madison ate cookies and the teacups waited in their box to be carried somewhere else. Her voice only broke twice. When she finished, Madison raised her mug of milk like a toast, and clinked it against Ava's.

"To quality control," Madison said.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a fair test, every other condition is kept the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one variable that was changed.
story:
Avery spread her wind turbine parts across the kitchen table like a surgeon laying out tools, which would have been more impressive if one of the tools wasn't a drinking straw. Her science fair project was due Friday, and the question on her poster read, "Does blade shape change how much electricity a model turbine makes?" She had three sets of blades: wide, narrow, and a weird curved pair she called The Scallops.

"Participation is voluntary, you know," said Muhammad, dropping into the chair across from her and stealing a pretzel. "Nobody is forcing you to build a wind farm at your kitchen table."

"Voluntary is not the same as optional," Avery said. "Ms. Ramos said the winner gets to demo their project at the assembly. In front of everyone. With the microphone."

"The microphone," Muhammad repeated, in the tone people usually save for the word "championship."

Avery clipped the wide blades onto the little turbine and set it in front of the box fan. She flipped the fan to high, and the multimeter jumped to a satisfying number. She wrote it down, swapped in the narrow blades, and ran it again. The reading was lower, almost half. Then The Scallops, which spun so enthusiastically that one blade flew off and landed in the fruit bowl. That reading was somewhere in between.

"See? Wide blades win," Avery said, already drafting her conclusion in pencil.

Muhammad frowned at her notebook. "Run it again. I want to watch the fan this time."

The second time, the wide blades gave a much smaller number than before. Avery stared at the two readings side by side, wide blades, same fan, same speed, different results. That should not happen. She leaned over the table and noticed that the fan had slid, probably when she'd grabbed the fruit bowl blade, so the turbine was now a hand's width farther away. The air reaching it was weaker.

"Oh no," she said. "The distance changed. That's not supposed to change."

"So what does that mean?" Muhammad asked, rescuing the escaped blade from an orange.

Avery thought about the birds that migrate past her window every fall, riding the same wind currents year after year because they know exactly which conditions they need. "It means my whole table of data is garbage. If I want to know whether blade shape makes a difference, everything else has to be the same. Same distance, same fan speed, same everything. Then the only thing left to cause a difference is the blades."

"Like a fair test," Muhammad said.

"Exactly like a fair test." She grabbed a ruler and taped a start line on the table. "New rule. The turbine never crosses this line, on pain of me yelling."

They ran all three blade sets three times each, careful as jewelers. The wide blades still won, but the margins were different, and The Scallops climbed into second place.
