Avery erased her old conclusion and started over, while Muhammad awarded the escaped blade a spot of honor balanced on the honey jar.

"Assembly microphone," he reminded her, spinning a straw turbine with his finger.

"Assembly microphone," Avery agreed, and clicked the pen.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
The living room was so crowded that Peyton had to sit on an overturned laundry basket, and Vihaan claimed the good armchair before anyone else could. Isla's grandpa had the couch corner, as always, holding the bowl of chips like a guard dog. At halftime he announced, for the third time that afternoon, that he remembered the very first Super Bowl like it was yesterday.

"Nobody remembers anything from 1967 like it was yesterday," Isla said. "That was before Dad was even born." She had been drafting a plan in her head since his first announcement: ask him specifics, and see whether the answers matched the real history she could look up on the tablet in her lap. A claim you couldn't see directly, she figured, was still a claim you could test.

"Fine, quiz me," Grandpa said. He leaned forward, and a chip fell into the cushion, where Vihaan's little brother, a total parasite who contributed nothing but commentary, grabbed it without shame.

"Who played?" Isla asked.

"Green Bay Packers against the Kansas City Chiefs," Grandpa said. "Everybody thinks it was always called the Super Bowl, but it took that name later." Isla typed and scrolled. He was right so far, and she was surprised enough to say so.

"Score?" she asked, because the score was where bluffers always cracked. She found a page that said the Packers won 35 to 10, played on January 15, 1967, and she waited.

"Thirty-five to ten," Grandpa said. "Packers." Peyton, from the laundry basket, said "no way" in the tone of someone who had lost a bet he hadn't made. Vihaan asked how anyone could remember a number from almost sixty years ago, and Grandpa just smiled and drank his soda.

The smile was ambiguous, Isla thought. Either proud or up to something. She remembered, then, a flashback from two summers ago, when she had found a shoebox in the attic marked KEEP and inside was a paper stub, orange and soft with age, that she had almost thrown out. She had asked Grandpa about it at the time and he had changed the subject so fast she'd gotten dizzy. She had assumed it was a bus ticket.

She went upstairs, found the box behind the old board games, and brought the stub down to the living room. It was a ticket, all right, with a date she now recognized: January 15, 1967. Section 14, Row 9. Grandpa took it from her with both hands.

"You were there?" Peyton shouted, tipping off the laundry basket.

"First one ever," Grandpa said. "Cheapest seat in the stadium, and worth every dime. Now somebody pass me the chips, because this halftime show is about to be terrible."

Vihaan handed him the bowl, and Isla sat down on the arm of the couch, right next to the only person in the room who had actually seen it.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
story:
Maria had been standing by the gym wall for exactly eleven minutes, and in that time she had learned one thing for certain: nobody was going to ask her to dance, and the night was not going to prolong itself.

The dance had started out as the best idea ever. Mya had texted her fourteen times about it, and Terry had promised to bring his ridiculous light-up sneakers, which he swore were "certified legendary." Maria had picked out her dress, practiced two dances in front of the mirror, and even arrived early. But then Mya got swept into a crowd by the snack table, Terry's sneakers got him surrounded by admirers, and Maria ended up alone beside the bleachers, watching.

That was when she noticed the spots.

They swept across the gym in slow, glittering curves, sliding over the floor, the basketball hoop, the backs of people's heads. Everyone danced inside them like they were snowflakes made of light. Maria frowned. There was only one spotlight, up on the stage, a single bright beam pointing at the big ball hanging from the ceiling. One beam. So where were all the spots coming from?

She watched the ball turn. Every time it rotated a little, the spots moved, all together, all in the same direction. When the ball stopped, the spots froze too. Maria's heart started going faster than the music. Each little mirror tile on the ball must be catching the spotlight and throwing the beam somewhere slightly different, so one light became hundreds of traveling spots. Hundreds! She looked around at everyone dancing in that broken-up light and felt like she was the only person in the gym who knew the secret.

"Where are they coming from?" asked a sixth grader next to her, staring at the spots sliding over her shoes.

"The mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots, because every tiny mirror tile reflects the beam in a different direction," Maria said. She pointed up at the ceiling. "Watch it stop. See? The spots stop too."

The sixth grader gasped like Maria had performed a magic trick. "That's the coolest thing I've ever heard."

"Excuse me," said a boy from her science class, appearing at Maria's elbow. "Did you just explain the lighting? Because that was awesome."

"It was inevitable," Terry announced, arriving with his sneakers flashing blue, then green, then purple. "Maria figures out everything. One time she found out who kept eating my lunch by tracking crumb patterns. The culprit was a very sneaky carnivore named Mya."

Mya appeared out of the snack crowd, cheeks pink. "The cookies had no defense!"

The DJ put on a song everybody screamed for, and the spots went sweeping across the floor like a hundred small invitations. The boy from science class held out his hand.

"So," he said. "Want to show me which tile is making that one spot by the door?"

Maria grinned and took his hand. "Race you to it."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel.
story:
Violet spread her pencils across the kitchen table like a hand of cards, trying to decide which twelve deserved a slice of her color wheel. The assignment was due Friday, and the wheel had to show symmetry, with red opposite green and blue opposite orange, so that every color faced its opposite like a mirror. The problem was that she had no idea why the order went red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet at all. Someone must have figured that out first, and it nagged at her the way a loose thread nags at a sweater.

Bradley arrived first, dumping his backpack on a chair. "You're still on that?" he said, eyeing her half-painted circle.

"Whoever made the first one had to start from nothing," Violet said. "No wheel to copy. That's the part I want to know."

Layton slid in beside her and started sorting the pencils into warm and cool piles without being asked. "You should allocate the good ones to the bigger slices," he said. "The cheap pencils will look streaky on the small ones anyway."

"That's actually smart," Violet admitted, and she felt a small pang, because Layton always had the smart ideas and she was the one who stayed up late with paint on her knuckles. She traded him a cookie for the sorting, which felt like a fair price, though it wasn't.

The three of them painted in a silence broken only by the scrape of brushes. When her blue bled into the yellow and made a smear of green, Violet nearly cried, but Layton blotted it with a paper towel before it spread. The wheel survived, mostly.

It was Mr. Dhillon, their neighbor, who cracked the question open. He came by to return Violet's mom's casserole dish, noticed the painted circle on the table, and said only, "You know, Newton has a whole book about color. It's on the shelf in my garage if you want it." He did not explain further, which was his way.

Violet found the book that evening, an old fat copy of Opticks, first published in 1704. She turned the pages at her own kitchen table, past diagrams of prisms, until she reached a drawing that stopped her cold: the colors of the spectrum arranged in a circle, an early form of the color wheel. Isaac Newton, the gravity man, had drawn this shape before anyone else thought to. She sat with that for a long moment, feeling oddly cheated and oddly thrilled at once, because now her wheel was a copy after all, and every wheel ever made was too.

She painted a tiny N in the center of her own circle, small enough that only she would notice it. Then she texted Bradley a photo of the page and waited, brush hovering, for the three dots to appear.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
story:
Maya stood in the laundry aisle of the grocery store with a crumpled list in her hand. Her mother was working a double shift, the basket at home was overflowing, and Maya had decided she would learn to do laundry herself before school on Monday. She picked up a bottle of detergent, read the back, and put it back. The second bottle promised something about colours, so she took that one.

At the end of the aisle, Ms. Ortiz from next door was comparing two boxes of dryer sheets. "First load?" she asked, nodding at the detergent.

"First load ever," Maya said. "I sorted everything into darks and lights already. I'm doing the darks first."

"Good plan," said Ms. Ortiz, and nothing more, which Maya appreciated. She paid at the register, lugged the bottle home, and loaded the washing machine with the pile of dark clothes: jeans, black t-shirts, her navy hoodie, and Rafaelle's grey hoodie, which he had left in her locker on Friday and told her she could borrow all weekend.

While the machine filled, Maya went through her own pockets by habit. A hair tie, a receipt, four cents. She dumped everything on the counter and shut the lid. The machine ran for forty minutes, and she used the time to fold a load her mother had left in the dryer, redoing a fitted sheet twice before the corners gave in. Folding, she decided, took more stamina than it looked like it would.

When she pulled the dark load out, she stopped. Every single item was speckled with tiny white shreds, dotted across the jeans, clinging to the hoodie sleeves, packed into the seams. She held up Rafaelle's grey hoodie and turned it over. Shreds everywhere. She turned her own pockets inside out, one by one. Clean. All clean.

She stood in front of the machine and thought. The shreds had to come from somewhere. They were on every item in the load, so whatever had made them had been inside the machine with the clothes. She had checked her pockets, so it had not been hers. Which left one hoodie she had not checked, because it was not hers to check.

She went back to Rafaelle's hoodie and felt along the front pocket. Inside, stuck to the lining, was the remains of a paper tissue, half dissolved, still shedding. It had broken apart in the wash, and its shreds had scattered over everything else. That, she realized, was why people checked pockets before washing, even pockets that belonged to other people.

She shook each item over the trash can, then ran the whole load through again with an extra rinse. Some shreds came off. The navy hoodie still held a few stubborn specks in its intricate stitching along the cuffs. She picked at them with tweezers and revised her plan for Monday: get the hoodie back to Rafaelle before he looked closely, or tell him first.

Monday morning, she found him at his locker with the hoodie folded over her arm, one last white speck still caught in the cuff. She held it out.

"You did laundry?" Rafaelle said. "Nice." He took the hoodie and started to put it on, then paused, his thumb finding the speck. "What's this?"

Maya took a breath. "Okay, so, whose tissue was in your pocket?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
story:
Harrison had always thought the clock in Grandpa's hallway was broken, because its ticking never matched the one in the kitchen. Now the house was quiet for a different reason, and both clocks had been stopped by an aunt with careful fingers, and Harrison stood between them not knowing what to do with his hands.

Saad and Walid had come with his mother for the gathering after the funeral, and the three of them ended up at the kitchen table, where a stack of folded papers sat beside a bowl of walnuts nobody was eating. "What are those?" Walid asked. "The one from the newspaper," Harrison said. "It's the obituary. It's the notice that runs in the paper when someone dies, with a short account of their life, their family and work and things like that." Saad pulled one from the stack and unfolded it, and Harrison read over his shoulder, expecting the version of Grandpa he already knew: retired machinist, three grandchildren, loved his garden.

Then he hit the word sailor.

"He was in the merchant marine," Harrison said slowly. "Two years. It says here he crossed the Atlantic eleven times." He looked up. "He never told me that. Not once. Not even when I did my boat project in fifth grade and he helped me sand the hull." Walid frowned. "Maybe the paper got it wrong. Papers get things wrong." Harrison stared at the small grey column, feeling the ground shift a little, because if the paper was right, then there was a whole Grandpa he had never met, and the only person who could ask was gone.

"So test it," Saad said. "If he was a sailor, there'd be stuff. Sailors leave stuff behind."

They started in the attic, where the July heat pressed down through the pink insulation between the rafters and everything smelled of cedar and dust. Under a trunk lid that took all three of them to lift, they found a folded chart of the North Atlantic with a soft crease worn molten-shiny from being opened and closed hundreds of times. They found a brass compass in a leather case, and a notebook with tide tables copied out by hand. "He kept this," Harrison said, turning the compass so the needle swung and settled. "He kept all of it, and he never said a word."

Downstairs, Mr. Chatterjee from next door was helping carry chairs, and when he spotted the compass in Harrison's hand he stopped in the doorway. "I wondered where that had gone," he said. "Your grandfather taught me to read that chart the summer I retired. Said a man who'd crossed an ocean eleven times could stand to teach one old neighbour a little navigation." He smiled at Harrison's face. "He never talked about it at the fence, though. Said the sea was private."

Harrison looked at the compass, then at Mr. Chatterjee. "Would you teach me now?" he asked.

"Every Saturday," Mr. Chatterjee said. "Bring the chart."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Luke sat cross-legged on the floor of Paul's bedroom, holding Paul's phone with both hands, staring at the group chat.

WHERE ARE YOU, the message said. He had typed it himself, all capitals, thirty seconds ago.

"You have to admit it stands out," Paul said, peeking over his shoulder. "Everything else in that chat is lowercase. Kendra writes entire sentences without a single capital. It's kind of a revolution in laziness."

Three dots appeared at the bottom of the screen. Then Kendra's reply came through: "why are you yelling at us?"

Luke frowned at the phone. "I wasn't yelling. I was typing."

"Doesn't matter," Paul said, taking a chip from the bag between them. "Everybody reads caps as shouting. That's just how it works. Type it again like a normal human."

Luke thought about that. The two of them were supposed to meet Kendra at the skate park at three, and it was already two-forty, and nobody had answered his first message, the polite lowercase one that said "hey we still on for today?" That message had sunk into the chat like a stone into a pond. The all-caps one had gotten a reply in under a minute.

So there was a rule here, and the rule had two sides. Quiet messages disappeared. Loud messages got noticed, but the people who noticed them thought you were angry at them. He could not see Kendra's face, could not hear her voice, and somehow the shape of the letters was doing the job of a tone of voice.

He tried an experiment. He typed: "sorry, not yelling, just late. are you still coming?"

Then, after a pause, he added a second message, all capitals: "AND BRING THE EXTRA WHEEL."

"See, now that second one just sounds like you're furious about a wheel," Paul said.

But the reply came fast. "lol ok. and why were you screaming at your phone earlier?" Then a string of laughing faces. Kendra had understood. The capitals were loud, but when you put them next to a calm message, the loudness turned into a joke instead of a fight.

Luke leaned back against Paul's bed and thought through what had just happened, because it felt bigger than one afternoon. At the park, Kendra would hear his actual voice, and his tone would come along for free. On the phone, tone had to be built out of letters and punctuation, and everyone had agreed on the meanings without ever saying them out loud. A period at the end of "ok" could feel cold. All caps could eliminate every other message on the screen. None of it was proportional to anything; nobody had actually raised a voice, and yet people got hurt or laughed or answered, all depending on shapes.

He typed one more message to test the idea: "MEETING AT THE USUAL SPOT."

Kendra answered before he even set the phone down. "stop SHOUTING and yes we're leaving now."

Paul grabbed his board off the wall hooks and pulled open the bedroom door. Luke stood, pocketed the phone, and followed him down the stairs into the bright afternoon.

"NEXT TIME," Luke said in his loudest voice, "I'LL JUST SEND A PIGEON."

"THAT'S STILL SHOUTING," Paul yelled back, and his little sister, passing through the kitchen, told them both to knock it off.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Brackets are cleared with the distributive property before solving: 3(x + 2) becomes 3x + 6, because the 3 multiplies both terms inside.
story:
Norah had fifteen minutes before her mom picked her up, so she spread her math sheet on the counter of the corner store beside the slurpee machine and got to work. The sheet was due tomorrow, and she had gotten every question right until the last one, which had brackets in it, and something about brackets made her brain fold in half.

Eliana slid in beside her with a bag of chips. "That one's easy. It's just three times x plus two, so three x plus two." She snapped a chip in half for emphasis.

Norah wrote 3x + 2, solved it, and got x equals three. Then she did what Ms. Chaudhry had drilled into them all week: she checked it. She substituted three back into the original equation, and the two sides came out different. Not close. Different. She erased so hard the paper went thin.

"See, it doesn't check," Norah said. "So something before the solving step went wrong." She looked at the brackets again. The three sat outside them like a guard. Maybe it wasn't just multiplying the x. She tried multiplying both things inside, so 3(x + 2) became 3x + 6, and solved from there. This time, when she substituted her answer back, both sides matched exactly.

"Wait, why?" Eliana leaned over the counter, chip forgotten.

"Because the three multiplies both terms inside," Norah said. "Not just the x. The two gets it too."

Charles-Edouard appeared from the magazine rack holding a wildlife magazine with a kangaroo on the cover. "That's a marsupial," he said, tapping the picture, "and that's the only thing I understand in this store." He squinted at their paper. "The cover says the photos depict animals in their natural habitat, which is more than I can say for math homework in a corner store."

Norah laughed, then copied the corrected steps into her notebook so she would remember. She wrote it out explicit and plain: clear the brackets first, then solve. She left out the part about feeling stupid, because she didn't, really. She had found the error herself, with the check, before the teacher could circle it in red.

Ms. Chaudhry came in for her evening coffee and paused at the counter. "Homework in my store now, Norah?"

"Last question," Norah said. "It almost beat me." She held up the sheet so the brackets showed. "But I got it. Want to check it?"

Ms. Chaudhry took a pen from behind the counter and substituted the answer back in, right there beside the candy display. "Checks out," she said, and dropped a coin on the counter for her coffee.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer; around December 21, it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
story:
Maria's problem was simple: on Friday she had to stand in front of Mr. Tang's science class and explain why we have seasons, and she did not understand it herself. She only knew the sentence she was supposed to memorize, which was about the tilt of Earth's axis, and memorizing felt like cheating.

On Tuesday she stayed after school with Hussain, who wanted the classroom's old globe for the chess club display he was building. He carried it to their table, and while he wiped dust off the stand with his sleeve, Maria turned the sphere slowly. Two dotted lines circled it, one above the equator and one below.

"What are these for?" she asked.

"No idea," Hussain said. "They're on every globe, though. My grandpa has one in his shop with the same lines."

Aedan, who was passing on his way to basketball practice and could never resist stopping where people were arguing, leaned over. "Those mark something. I read a page about it once." He pulled out his phone, tapped for a minute, and read aloud. "Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Around December 21, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn."

"So the top dotted line is the Tropic of Cancer," Maria said, "and the bottom one is the Tropic of Capricorn." She stopped turning the globe. The dates were June 21 and December 21. She knew those dates; they were the first day of summer and the first day of winter, at least where she lived. And the Cancer line was north of the equator, on her side of the world. She traced it with her finger, then the southern one. "When the Sun is overhead here, it's summer here. When it moves down to the other line, it's our winter."

"That's contagious, your face right now," Aedan said. "You look like you actually get it."

She borrowed the flashlight from Mr. Tang's desk, with a promise that returning it was an obligation she would not forget. She held it level and shone it straight down over the Tropic of Cancer, watching the light bunch into a small bright circle on the globe's surface. Then she kept the flashlight level and slid it down until the beam hit the Tropic of Capricorn. The bright circle followed. In her mind she added the axis, tilted, always tilted the same way, and saw the northern half leaning toward the light in one position and away from it in the other.

That night she wrote a message to Hussain, because he had taken the globe to chess club: "Don't let anyone draw on it. I need the two dotted lines visible on Friday. If your display contract with Mr. Tang says you can keep the globe all week, bring it to Room 12 before first period anyway. Maria."

On Friday she stood at the front with the globe and the flashlight. She shone the beam onto the dotted line in the north, said June 21, then moved the light to the southern line and said December 21, and watched Mr. Tang nod.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
story:
Benjamin sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field with his arm propped on his knee, the white cast making him look like he was wearing half a suit of armor. The doctor had printed out his X-ray, and he'd been staring at it all through math class, then through lunch, and now here, while his teammates ran drills without him. Hawa dropped onto the bench beside him, sweating and holding out half her granola bar.

"Look at this," Benjamin said, pointing at the film. "The bones glow white, and everything else is basically invisible. My whole arm, gone, except the bones." He turned the film toward the low sun, frowning. "I asked my little brother why, and he said the machine paints them. That can't be right."

Hawa leaned over and squinted. "My mom's a radiology tech. She told me once. The calcium in your bones absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them, so the bones show up white." She bit her granola bar. "Basically the machine can't see through the calcium, so that part stays white on the picture."

Benjamin went still. He stared at the X-ray again, and this time he wasn't looking at the forearm bones at all. He was looking at a small white smudge near his wrist, one he'd assumed was part of the break. "Hawa. Calcium is in the bone. So a white spot has to be something dense." He tapped the smudge with his finger. "That's separate from the fracture line."

"So? It's bone stuff," Hawa said.

"No, because." He stopped, thinking hard, the way he did in science when a whole chain of reasoning had to line up before he could say a word. "Three days after they put the cast on, the itch near my wrist drove me crazy, and I pushed a bottle cap under the edge to scratch with it. Then I couldn't get it out. I tried to incorporate it into my life, like, fine, I live with a bottle cap now. But metal is dense too. Denser than calcium, even."

Hawa snatched the film and held it up. "Benjamin. That is absolutely a bottle cap."

They ran, well, Benjamin jogged with his good arm pumping, straight across the field to where Ms. Johansson was coaching the younger kids. He explained, breathless, holding out the X-ray, and she laughed so hard she had to sit on her heels. At the clinic the next morning, the doctor tilted the film, looked at Benjamin over her glasses, and said, "Most kids draw on their casts. You gave me a mystery." She cut a small window, and out slid a battered bottle cap, defiant to the last.

Hawa held it up like a trophy. "Evidence," she said. "Case closed."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: In Hinduism, the soul passes through samsara, a cycle of birth, death and rebirth, and a person's karma, the results of their actions, shapes their next life.
story:
The temple smelled of sandalwood and marigolds, and Mia held her notebook against her chest so nobody would see the heading she had written at the bus stop: AFTER DEATH, TWO ANSWERS. Her grandmother had been buried nine days ago, and Mia's mother had said heaven, plainly, like closing a door. Then Courtney had said something about ghosts in science class, and Mia had begun to suspect that nobody actually knew. So when Raya invited her to the gathering for Raya's grandfather, Mia brought the notebook and a plan.

She found Raya by the shoe shelves, stacking sandals in pairs. "I'm sorry about your grandfather," Mia said.

"He'll be back," Raya said.

"Back from where?"

Raya picked up a stray sandal. "Back here. Another life." She said it the way Mia's mother said heaven, like a fact you didn't check.

Mia kept her skepticism to herself and followed Raya into the hall, where plates of food were being passed down long rows. She watched Raya's grandmother set a bowl of rice in front of a framed photograph, fold her hands, and stand there. Mia nudged Raya. "Is she monitoring something? Like, waiting for a sign?"

"She's offering food," Raya said. "For his next journey."

Mia wrote: not gone to a place, going to another life. She tested the idea out loud. "So your grandfather isn't in heaven watching you. He's going to be a baby somewhere."

"Maybe not a baby," Raya said. "But the soul gets born again. The cycle is called samsara."

"How does it pick?" Mia asked. "Where you go, what you become?"

Raya looked at her, then at the photograph. "Karma," she said. "What you did, what kind of person you were, that decides the next life. My grandfather was good, so it will be a good one."

Mia sat with that. A rule you couldn't see, working like gravity, sorting every soul after every death. Her grandmother had made jam for the whole street and never said a harsh word about anyone. Under Raya's rule, that had to count for something. Under her mother's rule, it counted too, just in a different place. She turned to a clean page and drew two columns, headed them both with her grandmother's name, and wrote heaven on one side and samsara on the other.

"It's for school," she said, when Raya leaned over her shoulder.

"It's for your grandmother," Raya said, and tapped the notebook. "What are you putting under karma?"

Mia thought of the jars of plum jam still lined up in the pantry, labeled in her grandmother's careful hand. She wrote: gave everything away. Then she underlined it twice, closed the notebook, and went to help carry the rice to the photograph.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
Anna had been standing at her grandfather's grave for ten minutes and still did not know what to do with her hands. The cemetery was quiet except for a crow somewhere behind the cedar hedge, and the granite marker in front of her looked the same as it had in March, gray and neutral and stubborn, as if it refused to admit anything had changed. She had brought tulips because her mother said flowers, and a scrub brush because she guessed dirt, but nobody had told her the order. Should the flowers come first, or the cleaning? She wondered whether there was a wrong way to do this, and whether her grandfather, who had opinions about everything from lawn mowing to lasagna, would let her feel it if she got it wrong.

Two rows over, a family of six appeared with rakes, buckets, and cloths, and they began working on an older grave as though they had done it a hundred times. Anna watched them sweep the stone, pull weeds from around the base, and wipe the carved letters until the names came back to life. Only after all of that did they set out small dishes of food and light sticks of incense. So that was the pattern: the cleaning had to precede the offerings. It made a kind of sense to her, the way you wash dishes before you set the table, and she felt a small spark of curiosity about where such a custom came from.

A girl about her own age knelt to brush leaves from the stone. Anna walked over, mostly to ask, and partly because watching them felt like borrowing someone else's courage. "Do you do this every year?" she asked.

"Every Qingming," the girl said, and when Anna's face must have looked blank, she added, "It's our festival, usually April fourth or fifth. Families go to their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings."

Anna thanked her and walked back to her grandfather. Her grandmother had died in February, and her grandfather had followed in June, and this whole year was a house with the furniture rearranged. She tested the idea she had just borrowed: she swept the brush across the top of the stone and watched dust and old rain streaks slide away. She worked the letters of his name one by one, GRAY letters first, then the rest, and the stone began to look like itself again. Her grandmother's name was on there too, underneath, and she cleaned that line as well, twice, carefully.

Then she set the tulips down and spoke out loud, quietly enough that only the crow and the granite could hear. "Okay. Now you." She stood with her palms flat on the warm stone until the other family's incense smoke drifted over on the breeze and curled around her wrists.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
The restaurant's big screen filled the whole back wall, and every table near it was packed. Laurence had saved seats for her parents, her little brother, Nash, Leyla, and her cousin Leo, who had flown in that afternoon from Nigeria. On the screen, the stadium camera panned across thousands of fans as the game went to a tense half-time break.

Then the crowd did the wave. A whole section stood, threw up their arms, and sat down, and the motion swept around the stadium like water running through a channel. Her brother scrambled onto his chair and shouted, "Do it here! Do the wave!" Nash stood. Leyla stood. Half the restaurant stood, and the wave wobbled its way down the counter and died somewhere near the kitchen door.

"It's called the Mexican wave," Leo said, sitting back down. "That's what everyone at home calls it."

"No way," Nash said. "It's just the wave."

"It's the Mexican wave," Leo insisted. "Ask anyone."

Laurence watched the screen instead of arguing. The commentators were replaying the crowd shots, and she noticed the ticker at the bottom, a line about the World Cup. A thought assembled itself in her head, slow and then sudden: if the move picked up its name at a World Cup, then people in different countries would have all learned it at the same time, from the same giant tournament, and their name for it would stick in their region. Leo calling it the Mexican wave and Nash calling it the wave wasn't a fight about who was right. It was two languages for the same thing, like two doors into the same room. She couldn't see the reason directly, but she could test it. She pulled out her phone under the table.

"Cheating," Leyla said.

"Researching." Laurence typed fast. There it was: the wave became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, which was why so many English speakers outside North America called it the Mexican wave. She held the screen up. "Look. Same move, different name, depending on where you watched it from. They're equivalent."

Nash read it twice and frowned. "So we're both right?"

"That's my consensus," Laurence said, and Leyla laughed so hard she knocked over the ketchup.

Leo looked almost disappointed. "I wanted to win."

"You can win the next round," Laurence said. "The waiter's coming, and I'm going to prescribe you the milkshake with the chili powder in it. House rule."

On the screen the second half kicked off, and the whole restaurant stood up again.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there.
story:
Hunter crouched in front of his sketchbook on the gallery bench, glaring at his drawing of Main Street. The road looked like it had melted. The buildings leaned toward each other like tired old men, and nothing went where it was supposed to go.

"You've erased that corner four times," said Isaak, who was supposed to be taking photos for the school newspaper before the gallery closed at five. "Also, your street is haunted."

"It's not haunted, it's crooked." Hunter flipped his pencil sideways and squinted down it like a tiny carpenter. "Mr. Fernando said something today about lines all going to one point. I was doodling a shark at the time."

"That shark was lush, though. Best shark I've ever seen."

"Thanks. Totally useless shark."

They had come to the gallery because Mr. Fernando had given the class a challenge: draw a street in one-point perspective, due tomorrow morning, and the only hints he'd offered were "come look at the big wall in the west room" and "bring a friend, less moping." It was quarter to four now, and the west room held a huge print of Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper.

Hunter stood in front of it. Long table, thirteen men, windows behind. He traced the ceiling lines with his finger in the air, then the tapestry edges on the walls, then the table's side. Every line, if he extended it in his head, ran to the same spot. He walked closer, then closer still, until a guard cleared his throat meaningfully.

"Right there," Hunter said. "The ceiling, the walls, the table. It all aims at his head."

"Whose head?"

"The guy in the middle. They all meet at the same point. That's what Mr. Fernando meant. One point. A vanishing point, like the street goes into it and disappears."

Isaak leaned in with his camera, hunting for his newspaper shot, and zoomed way past polite distance. "Wait. There's a tiny hole. Like somebody poked it with a pin. Dead center."

Hunter's brain did a fast, joyful tumble. If every line led there, and there was a hole there, then somebody had pinned something at that exact spot. Strings. Guide strings, stretched from the hole outward to keep the lines true. A tiny nail hole, still visible, in one of the most famous paintings on Earth.

He ran back to the bench and excavated his pencil case from the bottom of his backpack, sharpened the pencil with his teeth like a barbarian, and started a fresh street. He marked one dot first, then made every roofline, curb, and doorway run obediently toward it. The buildings stood up straight. The street went somewhere and vanished.

"Done," he announced at 4:58. "Photograph it before they kick us out."

Isaak snapped the picture, then offered a settlement: he'd text Hunter the photo, but only if Hunter drew him one lush shark, in perspective, by Friday.

"Deal," Hunter said, and drew a dot for the shark to vanish into.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines.
story:
Stella sharpened her pencil three times before she even touched the paper. Mr. Rodríguez had written "one-point perspective street scene" on the board and drawn a single dot in the middle of an example, and now everyone in the art room was supposed to make their own street plunge back toward that dot. Stella wanted hers to look like the road to her grandmother's house, with a bakery on the corner, but her first attempt had come out flat as a pancake. The buildings sat on top of the road instead of beside it.

"You look like you're about to boycott this assignment," Paige whispered from the next easel.

"I might," Stella said. "My street is broken."

Mr. Rodríguez walked past and paused at her table. He tapped the empty air above her drawing with one finger. "Draw your orthogonals first," he said, and moved on before Stella could ask what on earth those were.

Stella stared at the dot he had told her to mark, the vanishing point, sitting in the middle of her page like a tiny moon. Paige leaned over and slid a torn piece of sketchbook paper across the table. In round pencil letters it read: "I looked it up while he was talking. The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines. That's the whole secret. Your road edges have to aim at the dot. Claira already figured out the rooflines. Hurry up."

Stella read it twice. Then she looked at her drawing and saw the problem plainly: her road edges ran straight up and down the page, parallel, going nowhere. She flipped to a fresh sheet, marked her dot, and this time she started with those lines alone, the two road edges angling in toward the dot, then the curbs above them, then the long slope of a roofline on the bakery. It felt strange to draw a street with no buildings in it yet, only these slanted bones, but the bones were what held everything up. Where she had guessed wrong before, she could see it now: every line that was supposed to recede had been refusing to move.

She filled in the bakery between two rooflines, added the corner where her grandmother's mailbox would go, and even let herself draw a small green awning for the bakery window, carefully following the slant. At the next table Claira held up her own drawing so Stella could check it against hers. The toxic-yellow pencil Claira had used for her bus shelter looked almost warm against the gray street. Stella smiled and slid Paige's note back with one word added at the bottom: "Leisure is over. Look."

Paige read it, laughed quietly, and turned back to her own paper, drawing her first line straight toward the dot.
